claims.text: MnNiSi-based alloys can exhibit a high magnetocaloric effect.
The baseline MnNiSi-based alloy has poor mechanical toughness because of inherent brittleness.
Adding approximately 2 at% Cu and applying a two-step heat treatment will produce uniformly dispersed nanoscale Cu-rich precipitates at grain boundaries.
A solution treatment at approximately 1000°C will homogenize the Cu-containing alloy.
Aging at approximately 500°C will induce precipitation of Cu-rich phases.
The targeted Cu-rich precipitates can be maintained below 10 nm and confined to grain boundaries through optimized processing.
The Cu-rich precipitates will have coherent or semi-coherent interfaces with the MnNiSi matrix.
The nanoscale Cu-rich precipitates will act as a ductile phase.
The Cu-rich precipitates will strengthen the grain boundaries.
The Cu-rich precipitates will improve fracture resistance by deflecting or arresting crack propagation.
Limiting the concentration and spatial extent of Cu-rich precipitates will minimize interference with magnetic exchange interactions.
The Cu-microalloyed and heat-treated material will have significantly greater mechanical toughness than the conventionally processed baseline.
The intervention will improve ductility and fracture resistance.
The treated material will retain at least 90–95% of the baseline magnetocaloric performance.
Keeping Cu near 2 at% and optimizing the heat treatment will prevent precipitate coarsening or non-uniform distribution.
Departures from the proposed Cu content or processing window may disrupt the magnetic network.
Departures from the proposed Cu content or processing window may yield insufficient mechanical improvement.
The experimental comparator is a Cu-free MnNiSi-based sample processed under standard conditions.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant toughness improvement or a magnetocaloric-performance loss greater than 10% will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis compares magnetocaloric performance with an 'untreated alloy,' whereas the other fields define the baseline as conventionally or standard-heat-treated material. These are potentially different comparators, making the claimed percentage retention ambiguous.
